title: About me
goal: Introduce yourself — your name, where you're from, where you live and what languages you speak — and ask others the same.
intro:
In this unit you learn the personal pronouns and the present tense of **ہونا** (honā, 'to be'), the most important verb in Urdu. You'll also meet the main question words, so you can start asking things as well as answering.

Notice how Urdu says 'I am from Pakistan': میں پاکستان سے ہوں — literally 'I Pakistan from am'. The little word سے (se, 'from') comes *after* the noun: Urdu has **postpositions** instead of prepositions.

vocab.note: Spelled the same as میں meṃ 'in'.
Also often used to mean 'I' in some regions (Lucknow, UP).
Formal pronunciation 'voh'. Urdu doesn't distinguish he/she in pronouns — the verb shows gender.
m. Traditional Urdu name; بھارت bhārat is also used, especially in Pakistani media.
مجھے اردو آتی ہے = I know Urdu (lit. Urdu comes to me).
Comes after the word it refers to: میں بھی = me too.

phrases.native: میں تھوڑی تھوڑی اردو بولتا ہوں۔
phrases.roman: maiṃ thoṛī thoṛī urdū boltā hūṃ.

phrases.native: اس کو اردو میں کیا کہتے ہیں؟
phrases.roman: is ko urdū meṃ kyā kahte haiṃ?

grammar.title: Pronouns and the present of ہونا 'to be'
grammar.body:
The present tense of ہونا is short and must be learned by heart:

میں ہوں maiṃ hūṃ — I am
تو ہے tū hai — you are (intimate)
یہ / وہ ہے ye / vo hai — he, she, it is
ہم ہیں ham haiṃ — we are
تم ہو tum ho — you are (familiar)
آپ ہیں āp haiṃ — you are (polite)
یہ / وہ ہیں ye / vo haiṃ — they are; he/she is (respectful)

**یہ** is for people and things near you, **وہ** for those further away. Neither shows gender — 'he' and 'she' are the same word. To talk respectfully *about* someone (a parent, a teacher), use the plural ہیں even for one person: وہ میرے استاد ہیں 'he is my teacher'.

grammar.title: Asking questions
grammar.body:
**Yes/no questions** need no change in word order: just raise your voice at the end, or put **کیا** kyā at the start. (Here کیا does not mean 'what' — it just signals a question.)

**Question words** — کیا what, کون who, کہاں where, کب when, کیوں why, کیسا how — normally go **just before the verb**, in the same position as the answer would: آپ کہاں رہتے ہیں؟ 'you where live?' → میں کراچی میں رہتا ہوں 'I in Karachi live'.

Postpositions stick to question words too: کہاں سے 'from where', کس کا 'whose'.

examples.native: تم اردو کیوں سیکھ رہے ہو؟
examples.roman: tum urdū kyoṃ sīkh rahe ho?

dialogue.title: On the train to Islamabad
dialogue.setting: Emma, a visitor, chats with Faisal, the passenger next to her.

lines.speaker: Faisal
lines.native: السلام علیکم۔ کیا آپ اردو بولتی ہیں؟
lines.roman: assalāmu ʿalaikum. kyā āp urdū boltī haiṃ?

lines.speaker: Faisal
lines.native: واہ! آپ کا نام کیا ہے؟
lines.roman: vāh! āp kā nām kyā hai?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.native: میرا نام ایما ہے۔ اور آپ کا؟
lines.roman: merā nām Emā hai. aur āp kā?
lines.en: My name is Emma. And yours?

lines.speaker: Faisal
lines.native: میرا نام فیصل ہے۔ آپ کہاں سے ہیں؟
lines.roman: merā nām Faisal hai. āp kahāṃ se haiṃ?
lines.en: My name is Faisal. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.native: میں انگلینڈ سے ہوں، لیکن آج کل لاہور میں رہتی ہوں۔
lines.roman: maiṃ Inglainḍ se hūṃ, lekin āj kal Lāhaur meṃ rahtī hūṃ.
lines.en: I'm from England, but these days I live in Lahore.

lines.speaker: Faisal
lines.native: اچھا! میں بھی لاہور سے ہوں۔ کیا آپ پنجابی بھی بولتی ہیں؟
lines.roman: achchhā! maiṃ bhī Lāhaur se hūṃ. kyā āp panjābī bhī boltī haiṃ?
lines.en: Oh! I'm from Lahore too. Do you speak Punjabi as well?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.native: جی نہیں، صرف انگریزی اور تھوڑی اردو۔
lines.roman: jī nahīṃ, sirf angrezī aur thoṛī urdū.
lines.en: No, only English and a little Urdu.

lines.speaker: Faisal
lines.native: آپ کی اردو بہت اچھی ہے!
lines.roman: āp kī urdū bahut achchhī hai!

culture: Pakistanis are delighted when foreigners try Urdu, and you'll hear آپ کی اردو بہت اچھی ہے after two sentences. Most educated Pakistanis also speak English, and everyday Urdu is full of English words (پلیز، سوری، اوکے). Urdu is the mother tongue of only about 8% of Pakistanis — most speak Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashto, Saraiki or Balochi at home — but almost everyone uses Urdu as the common language.
